clinicalPearls: Produces small yellow-white punctate lesions at the level of the inner choroid and outer retina at the posterior pole
There is characteristically little or no vitritis, which helps distinguish it from multifocal choroiditis
Symptoms include blurred vision, scotomata, photopsia and metamorphopsia
The principal sight-threatening complication is choroidal neovascularisation
Lesions typically evolve into small atrophic, punched-out chorioretinal scars
Management is observation for inactive lesions, intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy for choroidal neovascularisation, and corticosteroids or immunosuppression for aggressive inflammation
reference.pathophysiology: PIC is an idiopathic inflammatory process affecting the inner choroid and outer retina that produces focal punctate lesions. Associated disruption and breaks in Bruch's membrane, together with the inflammatory environment, predispose to the growth of a choroidal neovascular membrane, which is the main threat to central vision. Individual lesions heal to leave atrophic chorioretinal scars.
additionalDifferentials: Myopic degeneration with lacquer cracks and neovascularisation
Neovascular age-related macular degeneration in older patients
additionalInvestigations: Dilated fundus examination to identify the punctate lesions
Optical coherence tomography to localise lesions and detect subretinal fluid or neovascularisation
Optical coherence tomography angiography to detect choroidal neovascularisation
Fluorescein angiography showing staining of lesions and leakage from any neovascular membrane
Indocyanine green angiography showing hypofluorescent spots
Investigations to exclude tuberculosis and syphilis
redFlags: New metamorphopsia, central scotoma or subretinal fluid or haemorrhage indicating choroidal neovascularisation
Rapid progression with heavy inflammation suggesting multifocal choroiditis
reference.prognosis: The outlook is good when the disease remains uncomplicated, but choroidal neovascularisation can cause significant central visual loss; prompt treatment of neovascularisation improves the outcome.
pitfalls: Missing choroidal neovascularisation, which requires regular Amsler and optical coherence tomography monitoring
Confusing it with multifocal choroiditis, which shows vitritis, or with myopic neovascularisation
Failing to exclude tuberculosis and syphilis
Delaying anti-VEGF treatment once neovascularisation develops
references: American Academy of Ophthalmology, Basic and Clinical Science Course: Uveitis and Ocular Inflammation
management: Treat sight-threatening choroidal neovascularisation, the principal complication, with intravitreal anti-VEGF injections
Use corticosteroids, systemic or periocular, and consider steroid-sparing immunosuppression for active inflammatory disease
Observe uncomplicated punctate lesions, which often heal to atrophic scars without treatment
Exclude tuberculosis and syphilis before starting immunosuppressive therapy
Monitor with optical coherence tomography and OCT angiography, and advise Amsler grid self-monitoring for new distortion
Refer to a medical retina or uveitis specialist for ongoing management
